reference_action: Struggling Monstera: repot with root room and draining soil, more light, reposition coir pole/ties to support stem not petiole. OP later reports new shoot.

sources.reason: Conditional brighter window, suitable draining mix and repotting match part of reference; no staking correction.
2:47–3:39 repots in airy peat/perlite with stem above soil; partial match amid peroxide/hydro rescue extras.
2:28 explicitly moves recovering plant to bright indirect light; partial light match, with unrelated Alocasia semi-hydro rescue.
Replants in aerated draining mixture and gentle sunlight; partial match despite lemon/rot rescue extras.
Rootbound section repots in slightly bigger pot; low-light section gives brighter indirect location.

actions.action: Assess light and relocate if unsuitable
Check soil moisture and water if dry
Lift pot and discard pooled water
Check temperature and relocate if unsuitable
Group plants or make pebble tray for low humidity
Repot into fresh medium for poor growth
Apply suitable organic feed during growing season
Inspect leaves with lens and wipe small pest populations
Cut completely dead or mouldy leaves retaining green ones

resolved.reason: Main causes appear among numerous possibilities. Light and repotting are buried in a broad checklist; the visibly incorrect petiole tie is unaddressed.

harmfulness.reason: “Retain leaves that are predominantly green” and checking moisture before watering reduce rescue mistakes. The advice emphasizes conditions before treatments, with few risky interventions.

specificity_accuracy.reason: Covers light, drainage and repotting among many diagnoses. It misses the photo-specific staking issue and cannot narrow the cause from the sparse question.

feasibility.reason: Most checks use ordinary tools, but the “ten easy steps” expand into many possible tasks. Following the full guide is substantially more involved than a focused rescue answer.

- paragraph: If you have a large collection of houseplants, it’s a good idea to separate a poorly one from the rest, until you have identified and resolved the problem.
    - heading "How to spot a poorly houseplant" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Work out what’s wrong with your plant in ten easy steps:"
    - figure "Low light levels have led to leggy growth on this Syngonium":
      - img "Image"
      - text: Low light levels have led to leggy growth on this
      - emphasis: Syngonium
    - list:
      - strong: Check there’s enough light
      - text: Weak, spindly growth, pale leaves and poor flowering are all signs that a plant isn’t getting
      - link "enough light":
        - /url: /advice/understanding-plants/how-plants-use-light-to-grow
      - text: . You might also see lower leaves turning yellow and falling.
      - button "Definition of Variegated": Variegated
      - text: plants kept in a shady spot might
      - link "revert":
        - /url: /problems/reversion
      - text: to green.
      - text: Bear in mind that over winter, when sunlight is weaker, many houseplants benefit from being moved closer to south- or west-facing windows. Wiping dust off leaves allows more sunlight to reach the leaf surface.
    - figure "Leaf scorch on the leaves of a rubber plant (Ficus elastica) caused by too much direct sunlight":
      - img "Image"
      - text: Leaf scorch on the leaves of a rubber plant (
      - emphasis: Ficus elastica)
      - text: caused by too much direct sunlight
    - list:
      - strong: Check for too much light
      - text: Strong, direct sunlight, such as from a south-facing window in summer, can cause brown scorched patches on leaves and give them a washed-out appearance.
      - text: Shrivelled leaves on
      - link "shade-loving plants":
        - /url: /plants/types/houseplants/houseplants-for-shady-rooms
      - text: are also a sign that the position is too sunny. On variegated leaves, sun scorch is more likely on the paler sections of leaf.
    - figure "Wilting and yellowing are common signs of underwatering":
      - img "Image"
      - generic: Wilting and yellowing are common signs of underwatering
    - list:
      - strong: Check there’s enough water
      - text: Wilted leaves, brown and crispy leaf edges and flowers that fade or fall quickly are all signs that a plant isn’t getting
      - link "enough water":
        - /url: /advice/understanding-plants/how-plants-absorb-water
      - text: . Unlike with overwatering (below), older leaves at the base of a dry plant will often yellow and fall first.
      - text: Insert your finger into the growing medium to check how moist it is a few centimetres down. If it is very dry, water your plant. Rather than watering regularly at set intervals, it is good practice to check the moisture levels and only water when necessary.
    - figure "This succulent has suffered stem rot and complete collapse due to overwatering":
      - img "Image"
      - generic: This succulent has suffered stem rot and complete collapse due to overwatering
    - list:
      - strong: Check for too much water
      - text: Overwatering can also cause wilting, and it’s easy to mistake this for a lack of water and drown a plant, especially over winter when growth slows. Lift your plant out of its pot to see if water has collected in the base, tipping away any excess. Choosing a peat-free
      - button "Definition of Compost": compost
      - text: ", or mixing your own, to match your plant’s needs will help avoid issues caused by watering. For example, a peat-free cacti and succulent mix will contain sand and/or grit to improve drainage."
      - text: Other signs of overwatering include old and new leaves yellowing and dropping at the same time, browning in the middle of leaves, mouldy patches on leaves and flowers, stem rot and dark, mushy roots. Regular overwatering can lead to
      - link "oedema":
        - /url: /problems/oedema
      - text: and whole plant collapse.
    - figure "Low temperatures have blackened the new shoots of this Impatiens":
      - img "Image"
      - text: Low temperatures have blackened the new shoots of this
      - emphasis: Impatiens
    - list:
      - strong: Check the temperature
      - text: Consult the plant’s label,
      - link "RHS Find a Plant":
        - /url: /plants/search-form
      - text: or a good houseplant book to check the specific temperature requirements of your plant, and consider if that’s what it’s getting.
      - text: Leaves wilting, rolling, bleaching and going crispy suggest a plant is suffering from heat stress – common in very hot rooms like conservatories in mid-summer. Blackened leaves, leaf droop and whole plant collapse are symptoms of cold damage – commonly seen in unheated rooms, like porches, over winter.
    - figure "Brown leaf tips and edges are a classic sign of low air humidity":
      - img "Image"
      - generic: Brown leaf tips and edges are a classic sign of low air humidity
    - list:
      - strong:
        - text: Check
        - button "Definition of Humidity": humidity
      - text: Low air humidity (dry air) is a common cause of problems on foliage houseplants, especially over winter when the heating is on. You might see shrivelled, crispy leaves with brown tips and edges, plus early dropping of leaves, buds and flowers. Kitchens and bathrooms generally have higher humidity than other rooms. Humidity levels around a plant can be increased by grouping plants together or placing them on trays of damp pebbles.
      - link "Grey mould":
        - /url: /disease/grey-mould
      - text: on leaves and flowers, and stem rots on
      - link "cacti and succulents":
        - /url: /plants/types/cacti-succulents
      - text: ", are signs the air is too moist, which is common in bathrooms."
    - figure "The yellowing of these hydrangea leaves indicates a nutrient deficiency":
      - img "Image"
      - generic: The yellowing of these hydrangea leaves indicates a nutrient deficiency
    - list:
      - strong: Check for nutrient deficiencies
      - text: Houseplants are often grown in the same pot for years and will quickly use up all the
      - button "Definition of Nutrients": nutrients
      - text: in their peat-free compost. If growth seems lacklustre and flowering is poor, your plant may benefit from being repotted into fresh peat-free compost. Growth can also be given a boost by applying a suitable organic, liquid feed during the
      - button "Definition of Growing season": growing season
      - text: . Watering with tap water if you live in a hard water area can lead to nutrient deficiencies. When possible, water with room-temperature rainwater.
      - text: See our
      - link "guide to nutrient deficiencies":
        - /url: /prevention-protection/nutrient-deficiencies
      - text: for more help.
    - figure "Mealybugs are commonly found on houseplants":
      - img "Image"
      - generic: Mealybugs are commonly found on houseplants
    - list:
      - strong: Check for insects
      - text: Visible to the naked eye but more easily seen with a hand lens or magnifying glass,
      - button "Definition of Sap": sap
      - text: "-sucking insects can affect a plant’s appearance and vigour. Small numbers are usually easy to pick or wipe off, so check plants regularly, especially newly bought plants. RHS advice pages on"
      - link "mealybugs":
        - /url: /biodiversity/mealybug
      - text: ","
      - link "scale":
        - /url: /biodiversity/scale-insects
      - text: ","
      - link "glasshouse thrips":
        - /url: /biodiversity/glasshouse-thrips
      - text: and
      - link "glasshouse red spider mite":
        - /url: /biodiversity/glasshouse-red-spider-mite
      - text: contain information on managing these insects, including biological controls.
    - figure "This cyclamen has been infected by grey mould (Botrytis cinerea)":
      - img "Image"
      - text: This cyclamen has been infected by grey mould (
      - emphasis: Botrytis cinerea
      - text: )
    - list:
      - strong: Check for disease
      - text: Houseplants can suffer from various diseases that affect their leaves, especially where
      - button "Definition of Ventilation": ventilation
      - text: is poor. A fuzzy, grey-brown covering on stems, leaves or flowers suggests
      - link "grey mould":
        - /url: /disease/grey-mould
      - text: is the problem. A white dusting on leaves suggests
      - link "powdery mildew":
        - /url: /disease/powdery-mildews
      - text: ", and dark spots with yellow margins suggests a fungal leaf spot. Improving ventilation, spacing and growing conditions will help avoid and control many fungal diseases. Using fungicides on houseplants is not recommended. Houseplants can also suffer from"
      - link "viruses":
        - /url: /disease/plant-viruses
      - text: .
    - figure "Calcium deposits on the leaves of this Calathea":
      - img "Image"
      - text: Calcium deposits on the leaves of this
      - emphasis: Calathea
    - list:
      - strong: Consider the growing environment
      - text: Plants kept near direct sources of heat, like radiators, often suffer scorched leaves, while draughts can cause leaf yellowing and dry leaf edges. If curtains are drawn on cold nights, plants on windowsills can suffer due to cold air being trapped between the window and curtain.
      - text: Pale spots are commonly caused by cleaning products and aerosols landing on leaves, while overhead watering with (hard) tap water can leave noticeable calcium deposits.
    - heading "Helping your poorly plant" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Once you have identified the problem, make adjustments to your care regime.
      - text: This might include increasing or decreasing watering, moving your plant to a sunnier, shadier, warmer or cooler spot, increasing
      - button "Definition of Humidity": humidity
      - text: ", repotting, feeding or treating a pest or disease problem. Sometimes it takes a combination of these to see a positive change. See our"
      - link "guide to growing houseplants":
        - /url: /plants/types/houseplants/growing-guide
      - text: for further advice.
      - text: Cut off any mouldy, shrivelled, completely brown or completely yellow leaves with secateurs, as these won’t recover. Retain leaves that are predominantly green until the plant has produced a fresh flush of leaves, or you could delay recovery.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Healthy houseplants rely on the right conditions rather than routine treatments, so focus on providing sufficient light, correct watering and suitable peat-free
      - button "Definition of Compost": compost
      - text: before adding feeds or controls. Our
      - link "Houseplant 101 video series":
        - /url: /plants/types/houseplants/houseplant-101
      - text: is a great place to get practical guidance on caring for your houseplants.
